reasoning_passages: At $950K, you'd be entering the house at zero liquid margin for anything unexpected. And old houses always have something unexpected.
The second discovery — the thing the inspector didn't catch — is almost a certainty in a 1940s house. That second thing could be $20K or $60K.
So the honest read on $950K: you can afford the purchase price. You likely can't afford the house in its actual need-state with no buffer.

The regret argument usually cuts one way in a bidding war — toward 'go higher.' The forget-about-it argument (what it feels like to be stressed about money for 3 years, snapping at your husband about the kitchen, cancelling vacations because the roof went earlier than expected) doesn't have the same emotional voice at 11pm the night before the deadline.
If you're going to counter, counter at your real number, not a compromise number.

If you land at $925K and lose: it's going to feel awful for two weeks. Then a house will come up that you can actually afford to fix, and the loss will quietly become one of those 'thank god we didn't' moments.
